paper_a.title: A motivated exposition of the proof of Tverberg's theorem

metadata.description: Both papers establish Tverberg's theorem (any (d+1)(r-1)+1 points in R^d admit an r-partition with intersecting convex hulls). Paper A is a motivated exposition of the standard Sarkaria/Barany route: lift to one extra dimension, repackage the r-fold equalities as a single vector equation in R^(r-1)(d+1), then invoke the Colorful Caratheodory theorem. Paper B (Barany 2021) gives a genuinely new proof: it first proves the a-general-position case by a 'moving the points' homotopy that maintains a Tverberg partition through finitely many singular values, controlled by determinants of an explicit (n+d) x (n+d) block matrix, and then deduces the general statement by a limit. Same theorem, fundamentally different proof technique => relation_type=AP.

matches.explanation: Both are Tverberg's theorem in its classical form: any (d+1)(r-1)+1 points in R^d admit a partition into r groups whose convex hulls share a common point. Paper A states it as its main theorem (paper-origin), paper B states it as the cited classical result (origin=external, attributed to Tverberg 1966) that the new argument re-proves. The B-side TP433.1 being external while A-side TP425.2 is paper-origin is itself signal for AP: paper B's contribution is a new proof of TP425.2 = TP433.1.

Radon's theorem: any d+2 points in R^d split into two sets with intersecting convex hulls. Paper A treats it as a paper-origin warm-up (proved in full as a stepping stone to Tverberg); paper B cites it as an external classical result and notes it is the r=2 case of Tverberg. Same statement, different role in the two papers.

Paper A defines the convex hull of finitely many points as the set of convex combinations. Paper B does not separately define convex hull but introduces the related notion of an 'r-divisible' set / 'Tverberg partition' via the intersection of conv X_p. These are the principal geometric objects of each paper but at different levels of granularity: A defines the building block (conv), B defines the property of interest (r-divisibility) directly in terms of conv. Conceptually parallel rather than identical.

Barany's Colorful Caratheodory theorem is the central external lemma in paper A's proof of Tverberg. Paper B's new proof avoids it entirely: it uses determinants of an explicit block matrix M and a homotopy argument instead. The absence of any Colorful Caratheodory analogue in paper B is precisely what makes paper B 'a new proof'. (Listed as a none entry on the A-side despite being origin=external because its absence in B is the structurally most informative fact about the AP relationship.)

Both are the proof of Tverberg's theorem, but the proof techniques are fundamentally different - this is the heart of the AP relationship. Paper A's PP425.2 reduces the partition problem to a single vector equation in R^(2d+2) via auxiliary vectors phi_{j,i} and applies Colorful Caratheodory (presented for r=3, with general r remarked). Paper B's PP433.5 proves the a-general-position case TP433.2 by combining the initial-set construction (AP433.1) with the inductive 'moving the points' step (TP433.3); PP433.6 then deduces TP433.1 from TP433.2 by Tverberg's standard limit argument. Same destination theorem, disjoint proof architectures.

Paper A's standalone proof of Radon's theorem (lift to R^{d+1}, take a linear dependence, split by sign) has no counterpart in paper B. Paper B only mentions Radon as an external citation and the r=2 case; it never reproves it. Radon-as-warm-up is part of A's expository character that B does not share.

Composite L2 entry attached to the L1 proof match (PP425.2 vs PP433.5+PP433.6). The two inner step DAGs are interestingly different: A's inner steps walk through (i) reformulate as system of equalities, (ii) lift to R^{d+1}, (iii) rewrite as one vector equation in R^{2d+2}, (iv) introduce phi_{j,i}, (v) verify 0 lies in conv of each color class, (vi) apply Barany's theorem and read off the partition. B's inner steps walk through (i) set up the homotopy and matrix M(t), (ii)-(iii) regularity/sign control on det M, (iv)-(vi) locate next singular value t_1 and identify unique vanishing index h, (vii)-(viii) build M-bar(t_1), expand by column h, pick the swap target j, (ix)-(x) advance to a new regular value and iterate to t=1. The decompositions correspond at the highest level (both reduce Tverberg to a manageable algebraic / combinatorial problem) but share essentially no individual steps; this is the L2 evidence behind the AP classification.

Both encode the defining 'common point of r convex hulls' condition as a system of affine combinations. Paper A's EP425.3 writes out the r=3 case explicitly (three group-sums of alpha_i p_i agree, three group-sums of alpha_i agree, total = 1). Paper B's EP433.1 writes the same system in compact form (z = sum_{x in X_p} alpha(x) x and 1 = sum_{x in X_p} alpha(x) for all p). EP433.1 is the r-fold generalisation of the equality system that paper A states only for r=3.

Paper A's two-set partition equality (the r=2/Radon version of the affine-combination system) has no separate counterpart in paper B - paper B writes the r-fold system directly (EP433.1) and never specialises to r=2.

The 'lifted-vector reformulation' p_i^+ = (p_i, 1) in R^{d+1} that fuses the two equalities of Radon into a single equation S_1^+ = S_2^+ is paper A's expository device for the lifting trick. Paper B's matrix M (DP433.6) does include rows of ones to encode the affine constraint, but the explicit lift-by-appending-1 framing is absent and not the technical engine of B's proof.

The auxiliary vectors phi_{1,i} = (p_i^+,0), phi_{2,i} = (0,p_i^+), phi_{3,i} = (-p_i^+,-p_i^+) in R^{2d+2} and the resulting single vector equation (2) are the algebraic core of A's Sarkaria-style proof. They have no analogue in B, whose technical machinery is the block matrix M and its determinants.

'a-general position' (algebraic independence of all dn coordinates over Q) is the genericity hypothesis on which paper B's whole argument is built; the general statement is then recovered by limit. Paper A makes no use of any genericity assumption - the Colorful Caratheodory route works for arbitrary point configurations directly.
'Proper partition' (1 <= |X_p| <= d+1) is paper B's structural constraint on the partitions tracked through the homotopy; it has no counterpart in A, which never tracks a partition along a path.

'Regular value t_0' is an artefact of B's moving-the-points argument (a t at which the current partition is r-divisible with strictly positive coefficients). No analogue in A's static, Colorful-Caratheodory-based proof.
'Singular value t_1' (the first t > t_0 at which some alpha_h vanishes or det M vanishes) is the core combinatorial event in B's homotopy. Absent from A.

The (n+d) x (n+d) block matrix M(P) - whose r blocks B_p have columns (a_i,1) for i in J_p, with -I_d blocks and rows of ones separating blocks - is the central computational object of paper B. Paper A uses no matrix; its algebra is the vector identity in R^{2d+2}.

'Tverberg in a-general position' is the genericity-restricted intermediate theorem that paper B actually proves directly (and from which TP433.1 follows by limit). Paper A does not split off such an intermediate - it proves the full statement in one shot via Colorful Caratheodory.

The 'inductive moving step' (if {b_1,a_1,...,a_n} is in a-general position and {a_1,...,a_n} is r-divisible then so is {b_1,a_2,...,a_n}) is the technical heart of B's new proof. Paper A has no incremental / homotopy structure, so no counterpart.

The 'affine intersection lemma' (for X in a-general position with proper partition P, the intersection of the affine hulls of X_p is a single point if |X|=n and empty if |X|<n) is the geometric backbone of B's argument and is cited from Barany 2021 / Barany-Soberon 2018. Paper A neither states nor uses anything resembling it. (origin=external in B but the underlying result is B-specific machinery, hence retained as a none rather than dropped.)
Nonsingularity of M and M_i for proper partitions in a-general position - a paper-original proposition that powers the determinant/Cramer arguments throughout B. Has no analogue in A's argument.
Sign claim det M(t_0) > 0 at regular values - a genericity-driven sign control specific to B's homotopy.
Uniqueness of the vanishing index h at a singular value - the combinatorial tightness that lets B execute a single swap rather than handle simultaneous events. No analogue in A.
Matrix-form equation M(alpha,z) = c that packs the affine combination system EP433.1 into a single linear system - specific to B's matrix machinery.
Linearity of det M_i(t) in t - a Cramer-rule-derived identity used by B to locate singular values explicitly. No analogue in A.
Singular value formula t* = det M_h(P,0) / (det M_h(P,0) - det M_h(P,1)) - the closed-form expression for the next swap time in B's homotopy.
Column-expansion identity for det M-bar(t_1) used to identify which block J the swapped index can move into - B-specific.

The initial-set construction (rotated regular simplices + origin + perturbation) that produces a starting r-divisible set in a-general position - a constructive ingredient with no analogue in A's existence-only argument.
The 'moving the points' algorithm itself - B's main constructive contribution. A's proof is non-constructive (existence via Colorful Caratheodory) and contains no algorithm.
The proofs of PrP433.1, ClP433.1, ClP433.2, and TP433.3 are the technical core of B's new argument and have no counterparts in A.
A's remark that the general-r case follows by the same r=3 argument is an exposition-style remark with no analogue in B (which handles general r uniformly via the matrix construction).

A's remark that Radon is the case r=2 of Tverberg is also flagged in B's text (TP433.4 carries the same parenthetical), but is a pure cross-reference rather than a load-bearing claim, so we record it as paper-A-only at the node level.
Compatibility of B's initial-set construction with a given B in a-general position - a remark internal to B's algorithm.
Finiteness of the singular values along the homotopy - essential to termination of B's algorithm but absent from A's framework.
